1	Training data contamination undermines the validity of Large Language Model (LLM) benchmark comparisons, yet existing detection methods stop at binary flags without quantifying score inflation or providing calibrated estimates. We investigate whether Item Response Theory (IRT) can separate genuine ability from contamination artifacts on existing benchmarks. Using controlled contamination injection across Qwen2.5 (0.5B--3B) and three benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-Challenge, GSM8K), we find that IRT ability estimation alone accounts for the majority of calibration gains: vanilla 2PL without any contamination parameter reduces calibration error by up to 53\% relative to raw scores. The calibration benefit arises from IRT's measurement structure, which separates stable capability from item-level noise regardless of whether contamination is explicitly modeled. To connect detection signals with this calibration framework, we develop ContamCal, a two-stage pipeline that uses training-free Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) for exposure-based item filtering, then fits a contamination-augmented IRT model (2PL+$\gamma$). Item filtering is necessary: without it, IRT on full MMLU (14k items) is ineffective ($\tau = 0.024$). Preliminary cross-family evidence from Llama-3.2-3B ($N=3$--$4$, single seed) suggests that calibrated MAE remains below 0.02 when pooling across architectures. The contamination parameter $\gamma$ provides exploratory diagnostic value: in independent per-domain analyses without multiple comparison correction, Social Sciences shows a significant negative effect ($\gamma = -0.57$, CI excluding zero) within the Qwen family, though domain-level patterns do not generalize across architectures. We further document that Min-K\%++ exhibits directional reversal at small model scales (Cohen's $d = -1.55$ to $-1.98$), where the signal is actively misleading rather than merely ineffective. Simulation studies establish that reliable $\gamma$ recovery requires signal AUC $\geq 0.55$ and $J \geq 50$, exposing a structural gap between current LLM evaluation practice and the statistical requirements for contamination diagnosis via IRT.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Benchmark scores drive model selection, resource allocation, and research priorities for large language models, yet training data contamination undermines the validity of these scores in ways that current evaluation cannot quantify \citep{hendrycks2021mmlu,chang2025benchmarking}. When models encounter test items during training, observed accuracy conflates genuine capability with memorization, and practitioners have no principled way to determine how much of a reported score reflects real understanding. The problem is compounded by the scale of modern training corpora: trillion-token web crawls make contamination pervasive and instance-level measurement infeasible \citep{oren2024proving}. Post-hoc calibration that quantifies contamination effects despite imperfect detection is therefore essential for trustworthy evaluation.

Two developments make this gap urgent. First, \citet{sun2025emperor} systematically evaluate twenty contamination mitigation strategies (rephrasing, option shuffling, dynamic benchmark regeneration, and others) and demonstrate that none restores clean performance after contamination has occurred. This result forecloses the ``prevent contamination'' approach for models already trained on unrestricted web data. Second, contamination-free benchmarks \citep{white2024livebench} offer a partial solution but sacrifice the comparability and institutional knowledge accumulated around established benchmarks. Dynamic regeneration of test items may also be contaminated within weeks as web crawlers index benchmark repositories \citep{dong_2024_cdd}. The field therefore needs post-hoc statistical tools that can separate genuine ability from contamination artifacts on existing benchmarks.

Detection methods such as Min-K\%++ \citep{zhang_2024_minkpp}, ConStat \citep{dekoninck2024constat}, and Kernel Divergence Signatures \citep{choi_2025_kds} can flag contaminated items but stop at detection. They do not quantify how much scores are inflated or produce adjusted scores with uncertainty estimates. Score adjustment methods like DCR \citep{xu2025dcr} provide point corrections without uncertainty quantification or a principled measurement framework. IRT-based evaluation frameworks \citep{polo_2024_tinybenchmarks,habba_2025_growing_pains} apply psychometric ability estimation to improve evaluation efficiency, but they treat all items as equally trustworthy and ignore contamination entirely \citep{lalor_2024_irt_nlp}. These two research threads have developed in isolation: detection papers end at binary flags, while IRT papers assume clean data. No existing method bridges detection signals and a measurement-theoretic calibration framework to produce decontaminated ability estimates with credible intervals.

This paper asks: does calibrating contaminated scores require accurate per-item detection, or can a principled measurement model separate ability from noise more generally? We develop ContamCal to investigate this question. Stage~1 fuses multiple detection signals into continuous per-item exposure scores via training-free Reciprocal Rank Fusion \citep{cormack_2009_rrf}, avoiding the meta-circularity of learned aggregators that would require the very contamination labels we lack. Stage~2 embeds these exposure scores as covariates in a contamination-augmented IRT model (2PL+$\gamma$) that jointly estimates latent ability $\theta$ and a domain-level contamination effect $\gamma_k$. Our experiments yield a clear empirical finding: IRT ability estimation itself accounts for the dominant calibration benefit. Vanilla 2PL without any contamination parameter reduces calibration error on ARC by 53\% (MAE from 0.034 to 0.016), comparable to the full 2PL+$\gamma$ model. The calibration comes from IRT's measurement structure, which separates stable capability from item-level noise regardless of contamination modeling. \section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Benchmark scores drive model selection, resource allocation, and research priorities for large language models, yet training data contamination undermines the validity of these scores in ways that current evaluation cannot quantify \citep{hendrycks2021mmlu,chang2025benchmarking}. When models encounter test items during training, observed accuracy conflates genuine capability with memorization, and practitioners have no principled way to determine how much of a reported score reflects real understanding. The problem is compounded by the scale of modern training corpora: trillion-token web crawls make contamination pervasive and instance-level measurement infeasible \citep{oren2024proving}. Post-hoc calibration that quantifies contamination effects despite imperfect detection is therefore essential for trustworthy evaluation.

Two developments make this gap urgent. First, \citet{sun2025emperor} systematically evaluate twenty contamination mitigation strategies (rephrasing, option shuffling, dynamic benchmark regeneration, and others) and demonstrate that none restores clean performance after contamination has occurred. Second, contamination-free benchmarks \citep{white2024livebench} offer a partial solution but sacrifice the comparability and institutional knowledge accumulated around established benchmarks. Dynamic regeneration of test items may also be contaminated within weeks as web crawlers index benchmark repositories \citep{dong_2024_cdd}. The field therefore needs post-hoc statistical tools that can separate genuine ability from contamination artifacts on existing benchmarks.

They do not quantify how much scores are inflated or produce adjusted scores with uncertainty estimates. Score adjustment methods like DCR \citep{xu2025dcr} provide point corrections without uncertainty quantification or a principled measurement framework. IRT-based evaluation frameworks \citep{polo_2024_tinybenchmarks,habba_2025_growing_pains} apply psychometric ability estimation to improve evaluation efficiency, but they treat all items as equally trustworthy and ignore contamination entirely \citep{lalor_2024_irt_nlp}. \section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Benchmark scores drive model selection, resource allocation, and research priorities for large language models, yet training data contamination undermines the validity of these scores in ways that current evaluation cannot quantify \citep{hendrycks2021mmlu,chang2025benchmarking}. When models encounter test items during training, observed accuracy conflates genuine capability with memorization, and practitioners have no principled way to determine how much of a reported score reflects real understanding. The problem is compounded by the scale of modern training corpora: trillion-token web crawls make contamination pervasive and instance-level measurement infeasible \citep{oren2024proving}. Post-hoc calibration that quantifies contamination effects despite imperfect detection is therefore essential for trustworthy evaluation.

Two developments make this gap urgent. First, \citet{sun2025emperor} systematically evaluate twenty contamination mitigation strategies (rephrasing, option shuffling, dynamic benchmark regeneration, and others) and demonstrate that none restores clean performance after contamination has occurred. This result forecloses the ``prevent contamination'' approach for models already trained on unrestricted web data. Second, contamination-free benchmarks \citep{white2024livebench} offer a partial solution but sacrifice the comparability and institutional knowledge accumulated around established benchmarks. Dynamic regeneration of test items may also be contaminated within weeks as web crawlers index benchmark repositories \citep{dong_2024_cdd}. The field therefore needs post-hoc statistical tools that can separate genuine ability from contamination artifacts on existing benchmarks.

Detection methods such as Min-K\%++ \citep{zhang_2024_minkpp}, ConStat \citep{dekoninck2024constat}, and Kernel Divergence Signatures \citep{choi_2025_kds} can flag contaminated items but stop at detection. They do not quantify how much scores are inflated or produce adjusted scores with uncertainty estimates. Score adjustment methods like DCR \citep{xu2025dcr} provide point corrections without uncertainty quantification or a principled measurement framework. IRT-based evaluation frameworks \citep{polo_2024_tinybenchmarks,habba_2025_growing_pains} apply psychometric ability estimation to improve evaluation efficiency, but they treat all items as equally trustworthy and ignore contamination entirely \citep{lalor_2024_irt_nlp}. These two research threads have developed in isolation: detection papers end at binary flags, while IRT papers assume clean data. No existing method bridges detection signals and a measurement-theoretic calibration framework to produce decontaminated ability estimates with credible intervals.

This paper asks: does calibrating contaminated scores require accurate per-item detection, or can a principled measurement model separate ability from noise more generally? We develop ContamCal to investigate this question. Stage~1 fuses multiple detection signals into continuous per-item exposure scores via training-free Reciprocal Rank Fusion \citep{cormack_2009_rrf}, avoiding the meta-circularity of learned aggregators that would require the very contamination labels we lack. Stage~2 embeds these exposure scores as covariates in a contamination-augmented IRT model (2PL+$\gamma$) that jointly estimates latent ability $\theta$ and a domain-level contamination effect $\gamma_k$. Raw accuracy is already well-calibrated; neither IRT nor $\gamma$-based correction improves upon it. The $\gamma$ parameter nonetheless provides diagnostic value: it confirms contamination existence (ARC CI excluding zero) and reveals domain-level heterogeneity within a model family, while the decomposition analysis explains \textit{why} aggregate scores remain robust despite item-level contamination.
